blocks.label: text
blocks.text: We communicated with Celltrion before June 30, 2024, regarding issues that led to the deficiencies identified in the September 30, 2024, complete response letter (CRL). Specifically, we sent Information requests (IRs) related to the issues identified in the September 30, 2024, CRL to Celltrion on March 26, 2024, and May 3, 2024, respectively, during the review cycle. After we reviewed your responses to the March 26, 2024, IR that we received on April 2, 2024, we identified deficiencies that were communicated as deficiencies 1 and 2 in the September 30, 2024, CRL. Regarding your responses to the May 3, 2024, IR that we received on May 13, 2024, your responses did not sufficiently address the deficiencies cited in the IR, which were communicated as deficiencies 3 and 4 in the September 30, 2024, CRL.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: As discussed at the late cycle meeting on April 19, 2024, following a CGMP inspection of Celltrion, Inc., Korea (FEI 3005241015), FDA conveyed certain deficiencies to the representative of the facility. On June 14, 2024, we sent you a letter indicating that we have identified deficiencies that preclude further discussion of labeling and anticipated postmarketing requirements (PMRs) and known postmarketing commitments (PMCs). As of June 30, 2024, there was an outstanding deficiency related to the inspection. The inspection was reclassified to Voluntary Action Indicated (VAI) on July 26, 2024, and therefore the September 30, 2024, CRL does not include such deficiency.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Importantly, as of June 30, 2024, there was also an ongoing scientific disagreement that precluded action at that time. Specifically, during the review cycle, one of the primary reviewers concluded that there were clinically meaningful differences between CT-P43 and US-Stelara that would preclude approval based on review of the safety data in the comparative clinical study. The review team carefully considered the issues raised by the reviewer and was not able to reach resolution by June 30, 2024. After a thorough reconsideration of the evidence, including by the cross-disciplinary team leader, the CRL issued on September 30, 2024, did not include any clinical deficiencies.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: CELLTRION proposes to conduct a Phase 3 randomized study in patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis comparing PK, efficacy and safety in subjects who receive switching treatment with US-licensed Stelara (US-Stelara) and CTP43 versus subjects who receive only US-Stelara. Does the FDA agree that the proposed study design is suitable to support a demonstration of interchangeability between CT-P43 and US-Stelara, in particular with specific respect to:
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: Primary endpoints, statistical analysis of primary endpoints
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Your overall proposal is consistent with the FDA guidance document "Considerations in Demonstrating Interchangeability With a Reference Product" in general.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: You intend to submit an original BLA seeking licensure of CT-P43 as a biosimilar to USlicensed Stelara. You also intend to submit a supplement to support demonstration of interchangeability for CT-P43.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The proposed clinical development program to support a demonstration that CT-P43 is biosimilar to US-licensed Stelara includes the following completed and ongoing clinical studies:
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: CT-P43 1.1: A randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, single-dose, pharmacokinetic (PK) similarity study conducted in two parts.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: o Part 1: A randomized, double-blind, 2-arm, parallel group, single dose study in 30 healthy subjects weighing 60-90 kg to evaluate initial safety [treatmentemergent adverse events (TEAEs), additional PK, safety, and immunogenicity of CT-P43] compared to that of EU-approved Stelara.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: o Part 2: A randomized, double-blind, 3-arm, parallel group, single dose in 240 healthy subjects weighing 60-90 kg to demonstrate similar PK, safety, and tolerability of CT-P43, US-licensed Stelara, and EU-approved Stelara.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: CT-P43 3.1: A randomized, double-blind, 2-arm, parallel group study to compare efficacy, PK, immunogenicity, and safety between CT-P43 and EU-approved Stelara in 509 subjects with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The clinical study you plan to conduct to support a demonstration that CT-P43 is interchangeable with US-licensed Stelara is the focus of this meeting:
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: CT-P43 3.2: A randomized, active-controlled, double-blind, multicenter, study to evaluate PK, efficacy, and overall safety, including immunogenicity, of treatment alternating US-licensed Stelara (45 mg) and CT-P43 (45 mg) compared to USlicensed Stelara (45 mg) in subjects with moderate to severe psoriasis.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: During Study CT-P43 3.2, approximately 468 adult subjects with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis who are candidates for phototherapy or systemic therapy, will be treated with US-licensed Stelara 45 mg dosed at Weeks 0 and 4 (Lead-in Period). Prior to randomization at Week 16, Psoriasis Area Severity Index (PASI) assessment will be conducted. Subjects who do not achieve at least PASI 50 response will be discontinued from the study. Subjects achieving at least PASI 50 will be randomized in 1:1 ratio to either continue treatment with US-licensed Stelara or be assigned to the switching arm, with all subjects receiving the study drug every 12 weeks (Switching Period). Subjects in the switching arm will undergo treatment by alternating between the proposed interchangeable product (CT-P43) and US-licensed Stelara. Switching will occur at Weeks 16 (to CT-P43), 28 (to US-licensed Stelara), and 40 (to CT-P43).
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Your proposed primary endpoints are maximum serum concentration (Cmax) and area under the concentration-time curve (AUCtau) between Week 40 and Week 52. You also propose PK-related secondary endpoints: time to maximum serum concentration (Tmax) between Week 40 and Week 52 and trough concentration (Ctrough) up to Week 52.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: You propose the following secondary efficacy endpoints:
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: PASI percent improvement from baseline through Week 52
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: proportion of subjects achieving PASI 50/75/90/100 through Week 52
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: static Physician's Global Assessment (sPGA) 0/1 at Week 52
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Safety assessments include laboratory monitoring, immunogenicity, and hypersensitivity assessment.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The proposed overall study design is acceptable. We agree that subjects who do not achieve PASI 50 response at Week 16 be discontinued from further dosing.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: However, we recommend that subjects who do not achieve PASI 75 at Week 28 also be discontinued from further dosing in order to protect non-responders from being exposed to the risks of treatment in the absence of clinically meaningful benefit.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: section_header
blocks.text: b. Study population and inclusion/exclusion criteria
section_path: b. Study population and inclusion/exclusion criteria
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: We agree with the proposed study population of adult subjects weighing between 60 to 90 kg with moderate to severe psoriasis who are candidates for phototherapy or systemic therapy [defined as a PASI score of ≥12, body surface area (BSA) involvement ≥10%, and a sPGA score of ≥3].
section_path: b. Study population and inclusion/exclusion criteria
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Subjects will receive a single subcutaneous injection of 45 mg/0.5 mL of USStelara via pre-filled syringe with safety guard (PFS) at Weeks 0 and 4, followed by one injection of 45 mg/0.5 mL US-Stelara or CT-P43 every 12 weeks. Your background package states that if a subject's weight changes to > 100 kg, the subject can receive 2 injections of 45 mg/0.5 mL US-Stelara or CT-P43 at the investigator's discretion.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The proposal to use the 45mg/0.5 mL PFS presentation for both dose levels is acceptable but will result in subjects >100 kg receiving twice as many injections. Perform safety, as well as efficacy, subgroup analyses for subjects ≤ 100 kg and >100 kg with particular attention to injection site reactions.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The durations of the lead-in and switching periods are acceptable.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: Primary endpoints, statistical analysis of primary endpoints
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: We agree with your primary endpoints of area under the concentration-time curve over the dosing interval between Weeks 40 and 52 (AUCtau, 40-52) and maximum serum concentration during the dosing interval Weeks 40 and 52 (Cmax, 40-52). You proposed that the primary PK statistical analysis "will be analyzed in the PK set who received all 5 doses (full) of the study drugs (only 45 mg) and maintain weight ≤100 kg during the study. Patients who receive 90 mg at any visit will not be included in the primary PK analysis. Patients who weighted >100 kg at any visit at or after Week 16 but were administered 45 mg at the investigator's discretion will be discussed on a case-by-case basis at the blinded Data Review Meeting (DRM) before unblinding for inclusion in the primary PK analysis". This proposal is reasonable.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: You proposed that "the statistical analysis of the log-transformed primary endpoints (AUCtau and Cmax, 40-52)" will be "An analysis of covariance (ANCOVA)… with a fixed effect of treatment (Switching vs. US-Stelara maintenance) and covariates as follows:
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: Anti-drug antibody (ADA) status at Week 16 (categorical value)
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: AUCtau, 4-16 or Cmax, 4-16 for the corresponding primary endpoint (continuous value)
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: Disease activity by PASI score at Week 16 (pre-dose); Log-transformed ratio of PASI score at Week 16 over PASI score at Week 0 (continuous scale)."
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Your proposed ANCOVA model is reasonable in general. We acknowledge that your proposal of using the log-transformed primary endpoints (AUCtau and Cmax, 40-52) is consistent with the recommendation of the FDA guidance document "Considerations in Demonstrating Interchangeability With a Reference Product." However, the development of anti-drug antibodies for biosimilar products may affect the PK data distribution and make the rationale of logtransformation not applicable.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Consider conducting an interim analysis to evaluate the distribution of the primary endpoints to ensure that the proposed data transformation (logtransformation) is appropriate for this study. The planned interim analysis should follow appropriate statistical principles and be adequately pre-specified in the protocol. Should you use an alternative statistical approach, provide justification in your analysis plan. In addition, how to handle concentration values below the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) should be clearly pre-specified in the protocol.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Secondary efficacy endpoints of percent improvement from baseline in PASI score and sPGA 0/1 at Week 52 are acceptable. We do not agree with PASI 50. We recommend PASI 75/90/100.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Secondary PK endpoints of time to maximum serum concentration during the dosing interval (Tmax, 40-52) and Trough concentration (Ctrough) are acceptable. ."
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The safety endpoints and monitoring plan are acceptable.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: You proposed that "Analysis of secondary endpoints will be conducted for all patients including the patients who weighted >100 kg at any visit." Your proposal

blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: "The full analysis set and the per protocol set play different roles in superiority trials (which seek to show the investigational product to be superior) and in equivalence or noninferiority trials (which seek to show the investigational product to be comparable). In superiority trials, the full analysis set is used in the primary analysis (apart from exceptional circumstances) because it tends to avoid over-optimistic estimates of efficacy resulting from a per protocol analysis. This is because the noncompliers included in the full analysis set will generally diminish the estimated treatment effect. However, in an equivalence or noninferiority trial, use of the full analysis set is generally not conservative and its role should be considered very carefully."

We do not accept the post hoc analysis in which the protein content was used as covariate because the 1.6-8.2% higher protein content in CT-P43 is unlikely to be the root cause of the observed higher exposure. The PK similarity study, along with the comparative analytical assessment, led to the residual uncertainties regarding our ability to conclude that CT-P43 could be biosimilar to US-Stelara.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: list_item
blocks.text: Based on the CT-P43 1.1 study results provided in the briefing document, the PK similarity between CT-P43, US-Stelara, and EU-Stelara was not established. Hence, we are concerned that the clinical data obtained from Studies CT-P43 1.1 and CT-P43 3.1 would not be sufficient to support a demonstration that there are no clinically meaningful differences between CT-P43 and US-Stelara because PK similarity has not been demonstrated and an adequate scientific bridge has not been established to support the relevance of clinical data generated with EUStelara to the assessment of biosimilarity.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The Agency explained that, from the CAA analysis, we had some residual uncertainties for which we are counting on the PK data to resolve, including the difference in charge where acidic variants were lower by 14% in CTP43 (in peaks 4a, 2, and 3) and identified as related to sialic acid content, and specifically the NGNA/NANA difference for which there is literature identifying that there are differences in immunogenicity due to preexisting antibodies to NGNA in some people. Regarding antibodies to NGNA, the Agency asked whether the immunogenicity assays were designed to be able to detect ADAs to NGNA and the sponsor clarified that the assays were not. Therefore, the
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: www.fda.gov Agency suggested exploring the possibility of ADAs to NGNA as one potential cause for the observed PK difference that may also explain the negative ADA patient PK data.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The Agency acknowledged that there is difference in protein content between CT-P43 and US- licensed Stelara and EU- approved Stelara and the Agency also acknowledged the post-hoc analysis using protein content as a covariate. The Agency stated that the protein content difference of 1.6% to 8.2% is unlikely to be the sole cause to produce the observed difference in PK and encouraged the Sponsor to explore the effect of residual uncertainties that could also impact PK.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The Sponsor inquired if they could conduct another 3-way PK similarity study. The Agency responded that there is no objection to the conduct of a new 3-way PK similarity study but the Sponsor must provide a justification to support the acceptability of the data from new 3-way PK similarity study in lieu of the current PK similarity study by providing details of the difference in quality attributes of the products used in the old and new PK similarity studies.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The Sponsor inquired whether the filing of BLA would not be possible (i.e., Refuse to file) based on the current analytical and clinical data package. blocks.label: text
blocks.text: As agreed by FDA in BPD Type 2 meeting held on February 26, 2020, CELLTRION intends to provide the data up to Week 28 for all subjects from Study CT-P43 3.1 which will include primary efficacy analysis (i.e., mean percent improvement from baseline in Psoriasis Area and Severity Index [PASI] score at Week 12) and 12 weeks of safety and immunogenicity data following the single transition (from reference product to CT-P43) together with datasets in standardized CDISC format (e.g., SDTM and ADaM) at the initial BLA submission. In addition, the follow-up safety data up to Week 52 for all subjects from Study CT-P43 3.1 will be provided in Section 5.3.5.3 Safety Update at the 4-Month Safety Update. Does the Agency agree and have any feedback with the proposed approach?

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: While we consider your proposal to provide data from the comparative clinical study (CT-P43 3.1) for all subjects up to Week 28 at the initial BLA submission and follow-up safety data for all subjects up to Week 52 at the 4-Month Safety Update, acceptable, you will first need to address residual uncertainties from the comparative analytical assessment and PK similarity study. blocks.text: As mentioned in Question 1, for the initial BLA submission, CELLTRION proposes to include two strengths of CT-P43 (45 mg and 90 mg) presented in PFS that can administer the same dosage in the approved indications that use Stelara® 45 mg and 90 mg in PFS. blocks.text: Under the Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA) (21 U.S.C. 355c), all applications for new active ingredients (which includes new salts and new fixed combinations), new indications, new dosage forms, new dosing regimens, or new routes of administration are required to contain a pediatric assessment to support dosing, safety, and effectiveness of the product for the claimed indication unless this requirement is waived, deferred, or inapplicable.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Section 505B(l) of the FD&C Act, added by section 7002(d)(2) of the Affordable Care Act, provides that a biosimilar product that has not been determined to be interchangeable with the reference product is considered to have a "new active ingredient" for purposes of PREA, and a pediatric assessment is required unless waived, deferred, or inapplicable.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: FDA encourages prospective biosimilar applicants to submit an initial pediatric study plan (iPSP) as early as practicable during product development. FDA recommends that you allow adequate time to reach agreement with FDA on the proposed iPSP prior to initiating your comparative clinical study.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Sections 505B(e)(2)(C) and 505B(e)(3) of the FD&C Act set forth a process lasting up to 210 days for reaching agreement with FDA on an iPSP. FDA encourages the sponsor to meet with FDA to discuss the details of the planned development program before submission of the iPSP. You must address PREA for every
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: www.fda.gov indication for which you seek licensure, and we encourage you to submit a comprehensive iPSP that addresses each indication. For indications for which the labeling for the reference product contains adequate pediatric information, you may be able to fulfill PREA requirements by satisfying the statutory requirements for biosimilarity and providing an adequate scientific justification for extrapolating the pediatric information from the reference product to your proposed product (see question and answer I.16 in the draft guidance for industry, New and Revised Draft Q&As on Biosimilar Development and the BPCI Act. For conditions of use for which the reference product does not have adequate pediatric information in its labeling, a waiver (full or partial), or a deferral, may be appropriate if certain criteria are met.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: After the iPSP is submitted, a sponsor must work with FDA to reach timely agreement on the plan, as required by section 505B(e)(2)-(3) of the FD&C Act. For additional guidance on the timing content, and submission of the iPSP, including an iPSP Template, please refer to the guidance for industry, Pediatric Study Plans: Content of and Process for Submitting Initial Pediatric Study Plans and Amended Pediatric Study Plans 2 . In addition, you may contact the Division of Pediatric and Maternal Health at 301-796-2200 or email Pedsdrugs@fda.hhs.gov It should be noted that requested deferrals or waivers in the initial PSP will not be formally granted or denied until the product is licensed.

blocks.text: Under section 745A(a) of the FD&C Act, electronic submissions "shall be submitted in such electronic format as specified by [FDA]." blocks.text: CELLTRION plans to publish Clinical Study Report (CSR) for Study CT-P43 3.1 up to Week 28 with an equivalence margin of [-15%, +15%] using 95% confidence interval (CI) for the primary efficacy endpoint, the equivalence margin for global submission. For US BLA, CELLTRION intends to submit the CSR but include the efficacy data in CTD sections including Section 2.5 (Clinical Overview) and Section 2.7.3 (Summary of Clinical Efficacy) analyzed with a margin of [-10%, +10%] using 90% CI in line with the discussion with the FDA. Does the FDA agree that the proposed analysis approach is appropriate to support BLA?

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Clarify whether different protocol versions were used at different sites or countries. The most recent protocol version submitted to the IND on August 24, 2021, does not indicate that alternate analysis plans are planned for different regulatory authority submissions. If different protocol versions were used at different sites, clarify whether there were any differences in inclusion/exclusion criteria, assessment scales or timing of assessments, or any other aspect of the protocol besides the statistical analysis plan among the versions in use. If multiple versions of the protocol were used to collect data for Study CT-P43 3.1, the Clinical Study Report (CSR) should address all of the final analysis plans that are planned for submission to regulatory authorities. We do not agree that the CSR can include only the analyses intended for the 'global' submissions, with the analyses intended for US regulatory submissions only included in the Clinical Overview and Summary of Clinical Efficacy.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: In particular, the CSR should include the analyses agreed upon by FDA and the sponsor as previously conveyed in the Special Protocol Assessment-No Agreement (June 3, 2020) and Study May Proceed (December 16, 2020) letters. blocks.text: Please be advised that an original 351(k) BLA will be subject to "the Program" under BsUFA II. Therefore, at an appropriate time, you should request a BPD Type 4 (pre351(k) BLA) meeting and be prepared to discuss and reach agreement with FDA on the content of a complete application, including preliminary discussions regarding the approach to developing the content for risk evaluation and mitigation strategies (REMS), where applicable, patient labeling (e.g., Medication Guide and Instructions For Use) and, where applicable, the development of a Formal Communication Plan. You and FDA may also reach agreement on submission of a limited number of minor application components to be submitted not later than 30 days after the submission of the original application. These submissions must be of a type that would not be expected to materially impact the ability of the review team to begin its review. All major components of the application are expected to be included in the original application and are not subject to agreement for late submission.
section_path: DISCUSSION OF THE CONTENT OF A COMPLETE APPLICATION

blocks.text: Include in your BPD Type 4 meeting package your proposals for 1) the content of a complete application and 2) any minor components to be submitted within 30 days after your original submission. blocks.text: Under the Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA) (21 U.S.C. 355c), all applications for new active ingredients (which includes new salts and new fixed combinations), new indications, new dosage forms, new dosing regimens, or new routes of administration are required to contain a pediatric assessment to support dosing, safety, and effectiveness of the product for the claimed indication unless this requirement is waived, deferred, or inapplicable.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: www.fda.gov Section 505B(l) of the FD&C Act, added by section 7002(d)(2) of the Affordable Care Act, provides that a biosimilar product that has not been determined to be interchangeable with the reference product is considered to have a "new active ingredient" for purposes of PREA, and a pediatric assessment is required unless waived, deferred, or inapplicable.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: FDA encourages prospective biosimilar applicants to submit an initial pediatric study plan (iPSP) as early as practicable during product development. FDA recommends that you allow adequate time to reach agreement with FDA on the proposed iPSP prior to initiating your comparative clinical study. Sections 505B(e)(2)(C) and 505B(e)(3) of the FD&C Act set forth a process lasting up to 210 days for reaching agreement with FDA on an iPSP. FDA encourages the sponsor to meet with FDA to discuss the details of the planned development program before submission of the iPSP. You must address PREA for every indication for which you seek licensure, and we encourage you to submit a comprehensive iPSP that addresses each indication. For additional information on how you may fulfill the requirement for pediatric assessments or investigations under PREA, see question and answer I.16 in the guidance for industry, Questions and Answers on Biosimilar Development and the BPCI Act.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: After the iPSP is submitted, a sponsor must work with FDA to reach timely agreement on the plan, as required by section 505B(e)(2)-(3) of the FD&C Act. For additional guidance on the timing content, and submission of the iPSP, including an iPSP Template, please refer to the guidance for industry, Pediatric Study Plans: Content of and Process for Submitting Initial Pediatric Study Plans and Amended Pediatric Study Plans 5 . In addition, you may contact the Division of Pediatric and Maternal Health at 301-796-2200 or email Pedsdrugs@fda.hhs.gov. It should be noted that requested deferrals or waivers in the initial PSP will not be formally granted or denied until the product is licensed.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Under section 745A(a) of the FD&C Act, electronic submissions "shall be submitted in such electronic format as specified by [FDA]." FDA has determined that study data contained in electronic submissions (i.e., NDAs, BLAs, ANDAs and INDs) must be in a format that the Agency can process, review, and archive. Currently, the Agency can process, review, and archive electronic submissions of clinical and nonclinical study data that use the standards specified in the Data Standards Catalog. 6
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: On December 17, 2014, FDA issued the guidance for industry Providing Electronic Submissions in Electronic Format - Standardized Study Data. This guidance describes
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: www.fda.gov the submission types, the standardized study data requirements, and when standardized study data are required. Further, it describes the availability of implementation support in the form of a technical specifications document, Study Data Technical Conformance Guide, as well as email access to the eData Team (cderedata@fda.hhs.gov) for specific questions related to study data standards. Standardized study data are required in marketing application submissions for clinical and nonclinical studies that started after December 17, 2016. Standardized study data are required in commercial IND application submissions for clinical and nonclinical studies that started after December 17, 2017. CDER has produced a Study Data Standards Resources web page 7 that provides specifications for sponsors regarding implementation and submission of clinical and nonclinical study data in a standardized format. This web page will be updated regularly to reflect CDER's growing experience in order to meet the needs of its reviewers.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: For commercial INDs, Standard for Exchange of Nonclinical Data (SEND) datasets are required to be submitted along with nonclinical study reports for study types that are modeled in an FDA-supported SEND Implementation Guide version. The FDA Data Standards Catalog, which can be found on the Study Data Standards Resources web page noted above, lists the supported SEND Implementation Guide versions and associated implementation dates.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Although the submission of study data in conformance to the standards listed in the FDA Data Standards Catalog will not be required in studies that started on or before December 17, 2016, CDER strongly encourages IND sponsors to use the FDA supported data standards for the submission of IND applications and marketing applications. The implementation of data standards should occur as early as possible in the product development lifecycle, so that data standards are accounted for in the design, conduct, and analysis of clinical and nonclinical studies. For clinical and nonclinical studies, IND sponsors should include a plan (e.g., in the IND) describing the submission of standardized study data to FDA. This study data standardization plan (see the FDA Study Data Technical Conformance Guide) will assist FDA in identifying potential data standardization issues early in the development program.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: If you have not previously submitted an eCTD submission or standardized study data, we encourage you to send us samples for validation following the instructions at FDA.gov. For general toxicology, supporting nonclinical toxicokinetic, and carcinogenicity studies, submit data in the Standards for the Exchange of Nonclinical Data (SEND) format. The validation of sample submissions tests conformance to FDA supported electronic submission and data standards; there is no scientific review of content.
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The Agency encourages submission of sample data for review before submission of the marketing application. These datasets will be reviewed only for conformance to
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: www.fda.gov standards, structure, and format. They will not be reviewed as a part of an application review. These datasets should represent datasets used for the phase 3 trials. The FDA Study Data Technical Conformance Guide (Section 7.2 eCTD Sample Submission pg. 30) includes the link to the instructions for submitting eCTD and sample data to the Agency. The Agency strongly encourages Sponsors to submit standardized sample data using the standards listed in the Data Standards Catalog referenced on the FDA Study Data Standards Resources web site. When submitting sample data sets, clearly identify them as such with SAMPLE STANDARDIZED DATASETS on the cover letter of your submission.

blocks.text: Does the Agency agree with the proposed method for handling missing data for primary efficacy endpoint of Study CT-P43 3.1?
blocks.speaker: regulator

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: No. We do not agree with your proposal to use a complete case analysis for the primary analysis. While we agree that when the amount of missing data is small, 251 missing data will have only a limited impact on the conclusions, we also think it is important to use an appropriate imputation method for the primary analysis, as the assumptions underlying a complete case analysis are not likely to be satisfied. While all methods of handling missing data have limitations and drawbacks, we recommend using a multiple imputation approach as the primary method of handling 256 missing data with supportive analyses that use alternate assumptions and a tipping point analysis. To ensure that these analyses are fully prespecified, we recommend including complete details regarding these methods in the protocol/statistical analysis plan.
blocks.speaker: regulator
